title: Multi-Cycle Datapath
summary: Splitting instruction execution into several shorter steps to share hardware, and the FSM that sequences them.

slides.markdown:
A multi-cycle datapath splits an instruction's execution across **several shorter clock cycles** instead of forcing everything into one long cycle. Each step does one piece of work — fetch, decode, execute, memory access, write-back — as its own cycle.

The payoff: because steps are separated in time, the same physical **ALU** can be reused for both address calculation *and* arithmetic, and the same **memory port** can serve both instruction fetch and data access — resources single-cycle designs had to duplicate to keep everything happening simultaneously.

Since one instruction now spans several cycles, results have to be **held somewhere** between steps — the datapath gains internal registers/latches purely for this bookkeeping:

![Multi-cycle datapath with internal registers holding values between steps](assets/multi-cycle-latches.svg)

A value computed in one cycle (say, the ALU's memory address) must sit in a latch, unchanged, until a later cycle actually uses it — these latches don't exist in single-cycle design at all, since everything happens in one cycle there.

assets.alt: Multi-cycle datapath with internal registers holding values between steps

slides.markdown:
Because each instruction only takes as many cycles as it genuinely needs, different instructions naturally take different amounts of time now — the key efficiency win over single-cycle. A register-register `add` might finish in **4 cycles** (fetch, decode, execute, write-back — no memory step needed), while a `load` needs **5** (an extra memory-access cycle).

This directly recovers the time single-cycle design wasted forcing every instruction to fit the slowest one's duration — simple instructions now genuinely finish sooner in real time.

Sequencing which step happens on which cycle is the job of a **finite state machine (FSM)** controller — each state corresponds to one step (fetch, decode, ...), and the FSM transitions to the next state each cycle, with the exact sequence depending on the instruction type currently being processed.

This is a direct, practical application of the FSM concept from digital logic ([finite-state-machines-hw](finite-state-machines-hw)) — the multi-cycle control unit *is* an FSM, not just analogous to one.

Three designs, three points on the same trade-off curve:

| | Single-cycle | Multi-cycle | Pipelined |
|---|---|---|---|
| Cycle length | One long, fixed cycle | Several shorter, uniform cycles | One short cycle, overlapped |
| Hardware reuse | None | High — shares ALU/memory | Duplicated per stage (no sharing) |
| Instructions in flight | One at a time, fully | One at a time, across steps | Several, overlapping |
| Throughput | Lowest | Better, but still one at a time | Near one instruction/cycle |

Each step solved the previous design's biggest waste: single-cycle wasted time on fast instructions; multi-cycle fixed that but still ran one instruction at a time; pipelining ([pipelining-fundamentals](pipelining-fundamentals)) overlaps instructions for real throughput gains.

Tracing `lw $t0, 8($s0)` (load) across a multi-cycle datapath's steps:

```
Cycle 1 (Fetch):   IR <- Mem[PC]; PC <- PC + 4
Cycle 2 (Decode):  A <- Reg[$s0]; ImmExt <- sign-extend(8)
Cycle 3 (Execute):  ALUOut <- A + ImmExt   # address = $s0 + 8
Cycle 4 (Memory):  MDR <- Mem[ALUOut]      # read from computed address
Cycle 5 (WriteBack): Reg[$t0] <- MDR
```

Notice **IR, A, ImmExt, ALUOut, and MDR** are exactly the internal latches from the diagram — each holds one cycle's result until a later cycle consumes it. A register-register `add` would skip the memory-access cycle entirely, finishing in 4 steps instead of 5.
